There he had said that none could <hi type="italic">come to him, except the Father draw him;</hi> here he saith, <hi type="italic">except it be given him of my Father,</hi> which shows that God <hi type="italic">draws</hi> souls by giving them grace and strength, and a heart to come, without which, such is the moral impotency of man, in his fallen state, that he <hi type="italic">cannot come.</hi> <div eID="gen27175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27176" type="x-p"/> 3. We have here their final apostasy from Christ hereupon: <hi type="italic">From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.66">v. 66</reference>. When we admit into our minds hard thoughts of the word and works of Christ, and conceive a secret dislike, and are willing to hear insinuations tending to their reproach, we are then <hi type="italic">entering into temptation;</hi> it is as the letting forth of water; it is <hi type="italic">looking back,</hi> which, if infinite mercy prevent not, will end in <hi type="italic">drawing back;</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">Obsta principiis—Take heed of the beginnings</hi> of apostasy. (1.) See here the <hi type="italic">backsliding</hi> of these <hi type="italic">disciples. Many of them went back</hi> to their houses, and families, and callings, which they had left for a time to follow him; <hi type="italic">went back,</hi> one to his farm and another to his merchandise; <hi type="italic">went back,</hi> as Orpah did, to their people, and to their gods, <reference osisRef="Ruth.1.15">Ruth i. 15</reference>. They had entered themselves in Christ's school, but they <hi type="italic">went back,</hi> did not only play truant for once, but took leave of him and his doctrine for ever. Note, The apostasy of Christ's disciples from him, though really a strange thing, yet has been such a common thing that we need not be surprised at it. Here were <hi type="italic">many</hi> that <hi type="italic">went back.</hi> It is often so; when some backslide many backslide with them; the disease is infectious. (2.) The occasion of this backsliding: <hi type="italic">From that time,</hi> from the time that Christ preached this comfortable doctrine, that he is the <hi type="italic">bread of life,</hi> and that those who by faith feed <hi type="italic">upon him</hi> shall live <hi type="italic">by him</hi> (which, one would think, should have engaged them to cleave more closely to him)—from <hi type="italic">that</hi> time they withdrew. Note, The corrupt and wicked heart of man often makes that an occasion of offence which is indeed matter of the greatest comfort. Christ foresaw that they would thus take offence at what he said, and yet he said it. That which is the undoubted word and truth of Christ must be faithfully delivered, whoever may be offended at it. Men's humours must be captivated to God's word, and not God's word accommodated to men's humours. (3.) The degree of their apostasy: <hi type="italic">They walked no more with him,</hi> returned no more to him and attended no more upon his ministry. It is hard for those who have been <hi type="italic">once enlightened,</hi> and have <hi type="italic">tasted the good word of God, if they fall away, to renew them again to repentance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.6.4-Heb.6.6">Heb. vi. 4-6</reference>. <div eID="gen27176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27177" type="x-p"/> II. This discourse was to others a <hi type="italic">savour of life unto life. Many went back,</hi> but, thanks be to God, all did not; even then the <hi type="italic">twelve</hi> stuck to him. Though the <hi type="italic">faith of some be overthrown,</hi> yet the <hi type="italic">foundation of God stands sure.</hi> Observe here, <div eID="gen27177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27178" type="x-p"/> 1. The affectionate question which Christ put to the twelve (<reference osisRef="John.6.67">v. 67</reference>): <hi type="italic">Will you also go away?</hi> He saith nothing to those who went back. <hi type="italic">If the unbelieving depart, let them depart;</hi> it was no great <hi type="italic">loss</hi> of those whom he never <hi type="italic">had;</hi> lightly come, lightly go; but he takes this occasion to speak to the twelve, to confirm them, and by trying their stedfastness the more to fix them: <hi type="italic">Will you also go away?</hi> (1.) "It is <hi type="italic">at your choice</hi> whether you will or no; if you will forsake me, now is the time, when so many do: it is an hour of temptation; if you will go back, go now." Note, Christ will detain none with him against their wills; his soldiers are volunteers, not pressed men. The twelve had now had time enough to try how they liked Christ and his doctrine, and that none of them might afterwards say that they were trepanned into discipleship, and if it were to do again they would not do it, he here allows them a power of revocation, and leaves them at their liberty; as <reference osisRef="Josh.25.15">Josh. xxiv. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ruth.1.15">Ruth i. 15</reference>. (2.) "It is <hi type="italic">at your peril</hi> if you do go away." If there was any secret inclination in the heart of any of them to depart from him, he stops it with this awakening question, "<hi type="italic">Wilt you also go away?</hi> Think not that you hang at as loose an end as they did, and may go away as easily as they could. They have not been so intimate with me as you have been, nor received so many favours from me; they are gone, but will <hi type="italic">you</hi> also go? Remember your character, and say, Whatever others do, we will never go away. <hi type="italic">Should such a man as I flee?</hi>" <reference osisRef="Neh.6.11">Neh. vi. 11</reference>. Note, The nearer we have been to Christ and the longer we have been with him, the more engagements we have laid ourselves under to him, the greater will be our sin if we desert him. (3.) "I have reason <hi type="italic">to think you will not.</hi> Will you go away? No, I have faster hold of you than so; <hi type="italic">I hope better things of you</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.9">Heb. vi. 9</reference>), for <hi type="italic">you are they that have continued with me,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Luke.22.28">Luke xxii. 28</reference>. When the apostasy of some is a grief to the Lord Jesus, the constancy of others is so much the more his honour, and he is pleased with it accordingly. Christ and believers know one another too well to part upon every displeasure. <div eID="gen27178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27179" type="x-p"/> 2. The believing reply which Peter, in the name of the rest, made to this question, <reference osisRef="John.6.68-John.6.69">v. 68, 69</reference>. Christ put the question to them, as Joshua put Israel to their choice whom they would serve, with design to draw out from them a promise to adhere to him, and it had the like effect. <hi type="italic">Nay, but we will serve the Lord,</hi> Peter was upon all occasions the <hi type="italic">mouth of the rest,</hi> not so much because he had more of his Master's ear than they, but because he had more tongue of his own; and what he said was sometimes approved and sometimes reprimanded (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.17">Matt. xvi. 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.23">23</reference>)—the common lot of those who are swift to speak. This here was well said, admirably well; and probably he said it by the direction, and with the express assent, of his fellow-disciples; at least he knew their mind, and spoke the sense of them all, and did not except Judas, for we must hope the best. <div eID="gen27179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27180" type="x-p"/> (1.) Here is a good resolution to adhere to Christ, and so expressed as to intimate that they would not entertain the least thought of leaving him: "<hi type="italic">Lord, to whom shall we go?</hi> It were folly to go from thee, unless we knew where to better ourselves; no, Lord, we like our choice too well to change." Note, Those who leave Christ would do well to consider to whom they will go, and whether they can expect to find rest and peace any where but in him. See <reference osisRef="Ps.73.27-Ps.73.28">Ps. lxxiii. 27, 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.9">Hos. ii. 9</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Whither shall we go?</hi> Shall we make our court to the world? It will certainly <hi type="italic">deceive</hi> us. Shall we return to sin? It will certainly <hi type="italic">destroy</hi> us. Shall we leave the <hi type="italic">fountain of living waters</hi> for <hi type="italic">broken cisterns?</hi>" The disciples resolve to continue their pursuit of life and happiness, and will have a guide to it, and will adhere to Christ as their guide, for they can never have a better. "Shall we go to the heathen philosophers, and become their disciples? They are become vain in their imaginations, and, professing themselves to be wise in other things, are become fools in religion. Shall we go to the scribes and Pharisees, and sit at their feet? What good can they do us who have made void the commandments of God by their traditions? Shall we go to Moses? He will send us back again to thee. Therefore, if ever we find the way to happiness, it must be in following thee." Note, Christ's holy religion appears to great advantage when it is compared with other institutions, for then it will be seen how far it excels them all. Let those who find fault with this religion find a better before they quit it. A divine teacher we must have; can we find a better than Christ? A divine revelation we cannot be without; if the scripture be not such a one, where else may we look for it? <div eID="gen27180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27181" type="x-p"/> (2.) Here is a good reason for this resolution. It was not the inconsiderate resolve of a blind affection, but the result of mature deliberation. The disciples were resolved never to go away from Christ, <div eID="gen27181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27182" type="x-p"/> [1.] Because of the <hi type="italic">advantage</hi> they promised themselves by him: <hi type="italic">Thou hast the words of eternal life.</hi> They themselves did not fully understand Christ's discourse, for as yet the doctrine of the cross was a riddle to them; but in the general they were satisfied that <hi type="italic">he had the words of eternal life,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That the word of his doctrine showed the way to <hi type="italic">eternal life,</hi> set it before us, and directed us what to do, that we might inherit it. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That the word of his <hi type="italic">determination</hi> must confer eternal life. His <hi type="italic">having the words of eternal life</hi> is the same with his having <hi type="italic">power to give eternal life to as many as were given him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.2">ch. xvii. 2</reference>. He had in the foregoing discourse assured <hi type="italic">eternal life</hi> to his followers; these disciples fastened upon this plain saying, and therefore resolved to stick to him, when the others overlooked this, and fastened upon the <hi type="italic">hard sayings,</hi> and therefore forsook him. Though we cannot account for every mystery, every obscurity, in Christ's doctrine, yet we know, in the general, that it is the word of eternal life, and therefore must live and die by it; for if we forsake Christ <hi type="italic">we forsake our own mercies.</hi> <div eID="gen27182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27183" type="x-p"/> [2.] Because of the assurance they had concerning him (<reference osisRef="John.6.69">v. 69</reference>): <hi type="italic">We believe, and are sure, that thou art that Christ.</hi> if he be the promised Messiah, he must <hi type="italic">bring in an everlasting righteousness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">Dan. ix. 24</reference>), and therefore has the <hi type="italic">words of eternal life,</hi> for <hi type="italic">righteousness reigns to eternal life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.5.21">Rom. v. 21</reference>. observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The <hi type="italic">doctrine</hi> they believed: that this Jesus was the Messiah promised to the fathers and expected by them, and that he was not a mere man, but the Son of the living God, the same to whom God had said, <hi type="italic">Thou art my Son,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.7">Ps. ii. 7</reference>. In times of temptation to apostasy it is good to have recourse to our first principles, and stick to them; and, if we faithfully abide by that which is <hi type="italic">past dispute,</hi> we shall be the better able both to <hi type="italic">find</hi> and to <hi type="italic">keep</hi> the truth in matters of doubtful disputation. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The <hi type="italic">degree</hi> of their faith: it rose up to a full assurance: <hi type="italic">We are sure.</hi> We have known it <hi type="italic">by experience;</hi> this is the best knowledge. We should take occasion from others' wavering to be so much the more established, especially in that which is the present truth. When we have so strong a faith in the gospel of Christ as boldly to venture our souls <hi type="italic">upon it,</hi> knowing <hi type="italic">whom we have believed,</hi> then, and not till then, we shall be willing to venture every thing else for it. <div eID="gen27183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27184" type="x-p"/> 3. The melancholy remark which our Lord Jesus made upon this reply of Peter's (<reference osisRef="John.6.70-John.6.71">v. 70, 71</reference>): <hi type="italic">Have not I chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?</hi> And the evangelist tells us whom he meant: <hi type="italic">he spoke of Judas Iscariot.</hi> Peter had undertaken for them all that they would be faithful to their Master. Now Christ does not condemn his charity (it is always good to hope the best), but he tacitly corrects his confidence. We must not be too sure concerning any. God knows those that are his; we do not. Observe here, (1.) Hypocrites and betrayers of Christ are no better than devils. Judas not only <hi type="italic">had</hi> a devil, but he <hi type="italic">was</hi> a devil. One of you is a <hi type="italic">false accuser;</hi> so <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">diabolos</hi></hi> sometimes signifies (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.3">2 Tim. iii. 3</reference>); and it is probable that Judas, when he sold his Master to the chief priests, represented him to them as a bad man, to justify himself in what he did. But I rather take it as we read it: <hi type="italic">He is a devil,</hi> a devil incarnate, a fallen apostle, as the devil a fallen angel. He is Satan, an adversary, an enemy to Christ. He is Abaddon, and Apollyon, a son of perdition. He was of his father the devil, did his lusts, was in his interests, as Cain, <reference osisRef="1John.3.12">1 John iii. 12</reference>. Those whose bodies were possessed by the devil are never called <hi type="italic">devils</hi> (<hi type="italic">demoniacs,</hi> but not <hi type="italic">devils</hi>); but Judas, into whose <hi type="italic">heart</hi> Satan entered, and filled it, is called a <hi type="italic">devil.</hi> (2.) Many that are <hi type="italic">seeming</hi> saints are <hi type="italic">real</hi> devils. Judas had as fair an outside as many of the apostles; his venom was, like that of the serpent, covered with a fine skin. He <hi type="italic">cast out devils,</hi> and appeared an enemy to the devil's kingdom, and yet was himself a devil all the while. Not only he <hi type="italic">will be</hi> one shortly, but he <hi type="italic">is one</hi> now. It is <hi type="italic">strange,</hi> and to be wondered at; Christ speaks of it with wonder: <hi type="italic">Have not I?</hi> It is <hi type="italic">sad,</hi> and to be lamented, that ever Christianity should be made a cloak to diabolism. (3.) The disguises of hypocrites, however they may deceive men, and put a cheat upon them, cannot deceive Christ, for his piercing eye sees through them. He can call those <hi type="italic">devils</hi> that call themselves <hi type="italic">Christians,</hi> like the prophet's greeting to Jeroboam's wife, when she came to him in masquerade (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.6">1 Kings xiv. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Come in, thou wife of Jeroboam.</hi> Christ's <hi type="italic">divine sight,</hi> far better than any <hi type="italic">double sight,</hi> can see spirits. (4.) There are those who are chosen by Christ to special services who yet prove false to him: <hi type="italic">I have chosen you</hi> to the <hi type="italic">apostleship,</hi> for it is expressly said that Judas was not chosen to eternal life (<reference osisRef="John.13.18">ch. xiii. 18</reference>), and yet one of <hi type="italic">you</hi> is a devil. Note, Advancement to places of honour and trust in the church is no certain evidence of saving grace. <hi type="italic">We have prophesied in thy name.</hi> (5.) In the most <hi type="italic">select</hi> societies on this side heaven it is no new thing to meet with those that are corrupt. Of the twelve that were chosen to an intimate conversation with an <hi type="italic">incarnate Deity,</hi> as great an honour and privilege as ever men were chosen to, one was an <hi type="italic">incarnate devil.</hi> The historian lays an emphasis upon this, that Judas was <hi type="italic">one of the twelve</hi> that were so dignified and distinguished. Let us not reject and unchurch the twelve because <hi type="italic">one of them is a devil,</hi> nor say that they are all cheats and hypocrites because one of them was so; let those that are so bear the blame, and not those who, while they are undiscovered, incorporate with them. There is a society within the veil into which no unclean thing shall enter, a church of first-born, in which are no <hi type="italic">false brethren.</hi>  <chapter eID="John.6"/> <div eID="gen27184" type="x-p"/>

entries.33bb10cbfb001281b049f6b1d12777c7afb9ce20: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15003"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 6</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.6.1-John.6.13">Joh 6:1-13</reference>. Five Thousand Miraculously Fed.</title> <div sID="gen28926" type="x-p"/> (See on <reference osisRef="Mark.6.31-Mark.6.44">Mr 6:31-44</reference>).<div eID="gen28926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28927" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15003"/><hi type="bold">3. a mountain--</hi>somewhere in that hilly range which skirts the east side of the lake. <div eID="gen28927" type="x-p"/>
entries.c7e60fdfeab777500badf7962cd1c231ec03ca99: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15004"/><div sID="gen28928" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15004"/><hi type="bold">4. passover ... was nigh--</hi>but for the reason mentioned (<reference osisRef="John.7.1">Joh 7:1</reference>), Jesus kept away from it, remaining in Galilee.<div eID="gen28928" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.6.14-John.6.21">Joh 6:14-21</reference>. Jesus Walks on the Sea.</title> <div sID="gen28929" type="x-p"/> (Also see on <reference osisRef="Mark.6.45-Mark.6.56">Mr 6:45-56</reference>). <div eID="gen28929" type="x-p"/>
entries.65b25a8a6c5a97bbc2362ef0956fbab073bea316: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15005"/><div sID="gen28930" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15005"/><hi type="bold">14-15. that prophet--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="John.1.21">Joh 1:21</reference>). <div eID="gen28930" type="x-p"/>
entries.4bb3efc20793470919bbdb1a56aa8989a5432f69: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15007"/><div sID="gen28932" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15007"/><hi type="bold">16-17. when even was come--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Mark.6.35">Mr 6:35</reference>).<div eID="gen28932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28933" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">entered into a ship--</hi>"constrained" to do so by their Master (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.22">Mt 14:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.6.45">Mr 6:45</reference>), in order to put an end to the misdirected excitement in His favor (<reference osisRef="John.6.15">Joh 6:15</reference>), into which the disciples themselves may have been somewhat drawn. The word "constrained" implies reluctance on their part, perhaps from unwillingness to part with their Master and embark at night, leaving Him alone on the mountain.<div eID="gen28933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28934" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">went--</hi>rather, "were proceeding."<div eID="gen28934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28935" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">toward Capernaum--</hi>Mark says (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.45">Mr 6:45</reference>), "unto Bethsaida," meaning "Bethsaida of Galilee" (<reference osisRef="John.12.21">Joh 12:21</reference>), on the west side of the lake. The place they left was of the same name (see on <reference osisRef="Mark.6.32">Mr 6:32</reference>).<div eID="gen28935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28936" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jesus was not come to them--</hi>They probably lingered in hopes of His still joining them, and so let the darkness come on. <div eID="gen28936" type="x-p"/>
entries.e12637cac193dce555a9ab869b92407eb098b8b7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15008"/><div sID="gen28937" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15008"/><hi type="bold">18-19. sea arose, &c.--</hi>and they were "now in the midst of it" (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.24">Mt 14:24</reference>). Mark adds the graphic and touching particular, "He saw them toiling in rowing" (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.48">Mr 6:48</reference>), putting forth all their strength to buffet the waves and bear on against a head wind, but to little effect. He saw this from His mountain-top, and through the darkness of the night, for His heart was all with them; yet would He not go to their relief till His own time came. <div eID="gen28937" type="x-p"/>
entries.7758e3388a52d22cde1dfa0429442837e644a230: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15010"/><div sID="gen28942" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15010"/><hi type="bold">20. It is I; be not afraid--</hi>Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.27">Mt 14:27</reference>) and Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.50">Mr 6:50</reference>) give before these exhilarating words, that to them well-known one, "Be of good cheer!" <div eID="gen28942" type="x-p"/>
entries.9475b411a02b309f03eabc82a2f79b6c3f2bf5d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15011"/><div sID="gen28943" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15011"/><hi type="bold">21. willingly received him into the ship--</hi>their first fears being now converted into wonder and delight.<div eID="gen28943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28944" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and immediately the ship was at the land--</hi>This additional miracle, for as such it is manifestly related, is recorded here alone. Yet all that is meant seems to be that as the storm was suddenly calmed, so the little bark--propelled by the secret power of the Lord of Nature now sailing in it--glided through the now unruffled waters, and while they were wrapt in wonder at what had happened, not heeding their rapid motion, was found at port, to their still further surprise. <div eID="gen28944" type="x-p"/>
entries.2c0b051dd2a1153825f41cd7066d42c64c6f9b33: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15012"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.6.22-John.6.71">Joh 6:22-71</reference>. Jesus Followed by the Multitudes to Capernaum, Discourses to Them in the Synagogue of the Bread of Life--Effect of This on Two Classes of the Disciples.</title> <div sID="gen28945" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15012"/>22-24. These verses are a little involved, from the Evangelist's desire to mention every circumstance, however minute, that might call up the scene as vividly to the reader as it stood before his own view.<div eID="gen28945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28946" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The day following--</hi>the miracle of the loaves, and the stormy night; the day on which they landed at Capernaum.<div eID="gen28946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28947" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the people which stood on the other side of the sea--</hi>not the whole multitude that had been fed, but only such of them as remained over night about the shore, that is, on the east side of the lake; for we are supposed to have come, with Jesus and His disciples in the ship, to the west side, to Capernaum.<div eID="gen28947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28948" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saw that there was none other boat there, &c.--</hi>The meaning is, the people had observed that there had been only one boat on the east side where they were; namely, the one in which the disciples had crossed at night to the other, the west side, and they had also observed that Jesus had not gone on board that boat, but His disciples had put off without Him: <div eID="gen28948" type="x-p"/>
entries.a6679cf714c5f1629176a7443c13542bdb7631dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15014"/><div sID="gen28951" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15014"/><hi type="bold">25. when they had found him on the other side--</hi>at Capernaum.<div eID="gen28951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28952" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they said, &c.--</hi>astonished at His being there, and wondering how He could have accomplished it, whether by land or water, and when He came; for being quite unaware of His having walked upon the sea and landed with the disciples in the ship, they could not see how, unless He had travelled all night round the head of the lake alone, He could have reached Capernaum, and even then, how He could have arrived before themselves. <div eID="gen28952" type="x-p"/>
entries.5520250889f21a226a26e4df5f74b819dadd588c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15015"/><div sID="gen28953" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15015"/><hi type="bold">26. Ye seek me, &c.--</hi>Jesus does not put them through their difficulty, says nothing of His treading on the waves of the sea, nor even notices their question, but takes advantage of the favorable moment for pointing out to them how forward, flippant, and superficial were their views, and how low their desires. "Ye seek Me not because ye saw the miracles"--literally, "the signs," that is, supernatural tokens of a higher presence, and a divine commission, "but because ye did eat of the loaves and were filled." From this He proceeds at once to that other Bread, just as, with the woman of Samaria, to that other Water (<reference osisRef="John.4.9-John.4.15">Joh 4:9-15</reference>). We should have supposed all that follows to have been delivered by the wayside, or wherever they happened first to meet. But from <reference osisRef="John.6.59">Joh 6:59</reference> we gather that they had probably met about the door of the synagogue--"for that was the day in which they assembled in their synagogues" [Lightfoot]--and that on being asked, at the close of the service, if He had any word of exhortation to the people, He had taken the two breads, the perishing and the living bread, for the subject of His profound and extraordinary discourse. <div eID="gen28953" type="x-p"/>
entries.33b724ea7728b5b6bc3207e30cd6108473b1c744: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15016"/><div sID="gen28954" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15016"/><hi type="bold">27. which the Son of man--</hi>taking that title of Himself which denoted His incarnate life.<div eID="gen28954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28955" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall give unto you--</hi>in the sense of <reference osisRef="John.6.51">Joh 6:51</reference>.<div eID="gen28955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28956" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">him hath God the Father sealed--</hi>marked out and authenticated for that transcendent office, to impart to the world the bread of an everlasting life, and this in the character of "the Son of man." <div eID="gen28956" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb768549894b770303b55dfcd6d5098df8ba00f8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15017"/><div sID="gen28957" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15017"/><hi type="bold">28-31. What shall we do ... the works of God--</hi>such works as God will approve. Different answers may be given to such a question, according to the spirit which prompts the inquiry. (See <reference osisRef="Hos.6.6-Hos.6.8">Ho 6:6-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.3.12-Luke.3.14">Lu 3:12-14</reference>). Here our Lord, knowing whom He had to deal with, shapes His reply accordingly. <div eID="gen28957" type="x-p"/>
entries.cc139f59de7e5cc665770ebbb0355ee884a85a66: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15021"/><div sID="gen28961" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15021"/><hi type="bold">32-33. Moses gave you not, &c.--</hi>"It was not Moses that gave you the manna, and even it was but from the lower heavens; 'but My Father giveth you the true bread,' and that 'from heaven.'" <div eID="gen28961" type="x-p"/>
entries.af9304b6e6559a65f123cae94425497acdb1880c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15023"/><div sID="gen28963" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15023"/><hi type="bold">34. Lord, evermore give us this bread--</hi>speaking now with a certain reverence (as at <reference osisRef="John.6.25">Joh 6:25</reference>), the perpetuity of the manna floating perhaps in their minds, and much like the Samaritan woman, when her eyes were but half opened, "Sir, give Me this water," &c. (<reference osisRef="John.4.15">Joh 4:15</reference>). <div eID="gen28963" type="x-p"/>
entries.42d874349dc84e6147fc6709425bdbd61daba8e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15024"/><div sID="gen28964" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15024"/><hi type="bold">35. I am the bread of life--</hi>Henceforth the discourse is all in the first person, "I," "Me," which occur in one form or other, as Stier reckons, thirty-five times.<div eID="gen28964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28965" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that cometh to me--</hi>to obtain what the soul craves, and as the only all-sufficient and ordained source of supply.<div eID="gen28965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28966" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hunger ... thirst--</hi>shall have conscious and abiding satisfaction. <div eID="gen28966" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a599956d44365dcbc3b37326ec8c87e2142af49: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15025"/><div sID="gen28967" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15025"/><hi type="bold">36. But ... ye have seen me, and believe not--</hi>seen Him not in His mere bodily presence, but in all the majesty of His life, His teaching, His works. <div eID="gen28967" type="x-p"/>
entries.1b1278e0a4ace2fa554da2cd3032568d0de11f69: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15026"/><div sID="gen28968" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15026"/><hi type="bold">37-40. All that, &c.--</hi>This comprehensive and very grand passage is expressed with a peculiar artistic precision. The opening general statement (<reference osisRef="John.6.37">Joh 6:37</reference>) consists of two members: (1) "All that the Father Giveth me shall come to me"--that is, "Though ye, as I told you, have no faith in Me, My errand into the world shall in no wise be defeated; for all that the Father giveth Me shall infallibly come to Me." Observe, what is given Him by the Father is expressed in the singular number and neuter gender--literally, "everything"; while those who come to Him are put in the masculine gender and singular number--"every one." The whole mass, so to speak, is gifted by the Father to the Son as a unity, which the Son evolves, one by one, in the execution of His trust. So <reference osisRef="John.17.2">Joh 17:2</reference>, "that He should give eternal life to all that which Thou hast given Him" [Bengel]. This "shall" expresses the glorious certainty of it, the Father being pledged to see to it that the gift be no empty mockery. (2) "And him that cometh to me I WILL IN NO WISE CAST OUT." As the former was the divine, this is just the human side of the same thing. True, the "coming" ones of the second clause are just the "given" ones of the first. But had our Lord merely said, "When those that have been given Me of My Father shall come to Me, I will receive them"--besides being very flat, the impression conveyed would have been quite different, sounding as if there were no other laws in operation, in the movement of sinners to Christ, but such as are wholly divine and inscrutable to us; whereas, though He does speak of it as a sublime certainty which men's refusals cannot frustrate, He speaks of that certainty as taking effect only by men's voluntary advances to Him and acceptance of Him--"Him that cometh to Me," "whosoever will," throwing the door wide open. Only it is not the simply willing, but the actually coming, whom He will not cast out; for the word here employed usually denotes arrival, as distinguished from the ordinary word, which rather expresses the act of coming (see <reference osisRef="John.8.42">Joh 8:42</reference>, Greek), [Webster and Wilkinson]. "In no wise" is an emphatic negative, to meet the fears of the timid (as in <reference osisRef="Rev.21.27">Re 21:27</reference>, to meet the presumption of the hardened). These, then, being the two members of the general opening statement, what follows is meant to take in both, <div eID="gen28968" type="x-p"/>
entries.4a325ee4b34622a9a85e5b8f974e3dad546082b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15030"/><div sID="gen28979" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15030"/><hi type="bold">41-46. Jews murmured--</hi>muttered, not in our Lord's hearing, but He knew it (<reference osisRef="John.6.43">Joh 6:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.2.25">Joh 2:25</reference>).<div eID="gen28979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28980" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he said, I am the bread, &c.--</hi>Missing the sense and glory of this, and having no relish for such sublimities, they harp upon the "Bread from heaven." "What can this mean? Do we not know all about Him--where, when, and of whom He was born? And yet He says He came down from heaven!" <div eID="gen28980" type="x-p"/>
entries.14f1a74432a7c7b82f4f8a8c273d762863198229: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15035"/><div sID="gen28991" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15035"/><hi type="bold">47-51. He that believeth, &c.--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="John.3.36">Joh 3:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.24">Joh 5:24</reference>). <div eID="gen28991" type="x-p"/>
entries.75a7917c2c2299c1133c409a90fa2bf02ac2eb8b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15039"/><div sID="gen28996" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15039"/><hi type="bold">52. Jews strove among themselves--</hi>arguing the point together.<div eID="gen28996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28997" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">How can, &c.--</hi>that is, Give us His flesh to eat? Absurd. <div eID="gen28997" type="x-p"/>
entries.f58101ebef1e516869163eb4aa4dc2f091e4d6ea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15040"/><div sID="gen28998" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15040"/><hi type="bold">53-58. Except ye eat the flesh ... and drink the blood ... no life, &c.--</hi>The harshest word He had yet uttered in their ears. They asked how it was possible to eat His flesh. He answers, with great solemnity, "It is indispensable." Yet even here a thoughtful hearer might find something to temper the harshness. He says they must not only "eat His flesh" but "drink His blood," which could not but suggest the idea of His death--implied in the separation of one's flesh from his blood. And as He had already hinted that it was to be something very different from a natural death, saying, "My flesh I will give for the life of the world" (<reference osisRef="John.6.51">Joh 6:51</reference>), it must have been pretty plain to candid hearers that He meant something above the gross idea which the bare terms expressed. And farther, when He added that they "had no life in them unless they thus ate and drank," it was impossible they should think He meant that the temporal life they were then living was dependent on their eating and drinking, in this gross sense, His flesh and blood. Yet the whole statement was certainly confounding, and beyond doubt was meant to be so. Our Lord had told them that in spite of all they had "seen" in Him, they "did not believe" (<reference osisRef="John.6.36">Joh 6:36</reference>). For their conviction therefore he does not here lay Himself out; but having the ear not only of them but of the more candid and thoughtful in the crowded synagogue, and the miracle of the loaves having led up to the most exalted of all views of His Person and Office, He takes advantage of their very difficulties and objections to announce, for all time, those most profound truths which are here expressed, regardless of the disgust of the unteachable, and the prejudices even of the most sincere, which His language would seem only designed to deepen. The truth really conveyed here is no other than that expressed in <reference osisRef="John.6.51">Joh 6:51</reference>, though in more emphatic terms--that He Himself, in the virtue of His sacrificial death, is the spiritual and eternal life of men; and that unless men voluntarily appropriate to themselves this death, in its sacrificial virtue, so as to become the very life and nourishment of their inner man, they have no spiritual and eternal life at all. Not as if His death were the only thing of value, but it is what gives all else in Christ's Incarnate Person, Life, and Office, their whole value to us sinners. <div eID="gen28998" type="x-p"/>
entries.7505662b65b62be7e6cd3ebc0531108d89e3f53e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15045"/><div sID="gen29006" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15045"/><hi type="bold">59. These things said he in the synagogue--</hi>which seems to imply that what follows took place after the congregation had broken up. <div eID="gen29006" type="x-p"/>
entries.5fe428bc720634cbcf435b5cc81245be49e88718: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15046"/><div sID="gen29007" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15046"/><hi type="bold">60-65. Many ... of his disciples--</hi>His pretty constant followers, though an outer circle of them.<div eID="gen29007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29008" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hard saying--</hi>not merely harsh, but insufferable, as the word often means in the Old Testament.<div eID="gen29008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29009" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who can hear--</hi>submit to listen to it. <div eID="gen29009" type="x-p"/>
entries.34757cd924a5476e1610f3beedb41872e8bf2402: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15051"/><div sID="gen29016" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15051"/><hi type="bold">66-71. From that time, &c.--</hi>or, in consequence of this. Those last words of our Lord seemed to have given them the finishing stroke--they could not stand it any longer.<div eID="gen29016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29017" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">walked no more--</hi>Many a journey, it may be, they had taken with Him, but now they gave Him up finally! <div eID="gen29017" type="x-p"/>

entries.dada811120eb4eb1b7d82f7f3db6ed09e8e05ee0: <div eID="gen41833" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen41834" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen41835" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen41835" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen41834" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen41836" type="x-p"/> Jesus passes the sea of Tiberias, and a great multitude follow him, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.1-Joh.6.4">Joh 6:1-4</reference>. He feeds five thousand with five loaves, and two fishes, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.5-Joh.6.13">Joh 6:5-13</reference>. They acknowledge him to be the prophet that should come into the world, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.14">Joh 6:14</reference>. They purpose to force him to become their king; and he withdraws from the multitude, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.15">Joh 6:15</reference>. The disciples take ship, and go towards Capernaum, and are overtaken with a storm, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.16-Joh.6.18">Joh 6:16-18</reference>. Christ comes to them, walking upon the water, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.19-Joh.6.21">Joh 6:19-21</reference>. The people take boats and follow him, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.22-Joh.6.24">Joh 6:22-24</reference>. He reproves their fleshly motives, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.25-Joh.6.27">Joh 6:25-27</reference>. They profess a desire to be instructed, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.28">Joh 6:28</reference>. Christ preaches to them, and shows them that he is the bread of life, and that they who reject him are without excuse, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.29-Joh.6.40">Joh 6:29-40</reference>. They are offended, and cavil, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.41">Joh 6:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.42">Joh 6:42</reference>. He asserts and illustrates his foregoing discourse, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.43-Joh.6.51">Joh 6:43-51</reference>. They again cavil, and Christ gives farther explanations, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.52-Joh.6.59">Joh 6:52-59</reference>. Several of the disciples are stumbled at his assertion, that unless they ate his flesh and drank his blood they could not have life, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.60">Joh 6:60</reference>. He shows them that his words are to be spiritually understood, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.61-Joh.6.65">Joh 6:61-65</reference>. Several of them withdraw from him, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.66">Joh 6:66</reference>. He questions the twelve, whether they also were disposed to forsake him, and Peter answers for the whole, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.67-Joh.6.69">Joh 6:67-69</reference>. Christ exposes the perfidy of Judas, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.70">Joh 6:70</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.71">Joh 6:71</reference>. <div eID="gen41836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41837" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen41837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41838" type="x-p"/> After these things - This is a sort of indefinite expression, from which me can gather nothing relative to the time in which these things happened. It refers no doubt to transactions in the preceding year. <div eID="gen41838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41839" type="x-p"/> Jesus went over the sea of Galilee - Or, as some translate the words, by the side of the sea of Galilee. From Luke, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.10">Luk 9:10</reference>, we learn that this was a desert place in the vicinity of Bethsaida. The sea of Galilee, Genesaret, and Tiberias, are the same in the New Testament with the sea of Cinnereth in the Old. Tiberias was a city in Galilee, situated on the western side of the lake. See on <reference osisRef="Joh.6.22">Joh 6:22</reference> (note).
entries.3c1350760ee6b785f6c2b1dc2371d7af3954cb21: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen41839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41840" type="x-p"/> They saw his miracles which he did - John does not mention these miracles; but Matthew details them, Matthew 12:2-14:13. John seems more intent on supplying the deficiencies of the other evangelists than in writing a connected history himself.
entries.4bfb4d962ef4d94815db2337644f5d2010f67974: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen41840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41841" type="x-p"/> Went up into a mountain - This mountain must have been in the desert of Bethsaida, in the territories of Philip, tetrarch of Galilee. Our Lord withdrew to this place for a little rest; for he and his disciples had been so thronged with the multitudes, continually coming and going, that they had not time to take necessary food. See <reference osisRef="Mar.6.31">Mar 6:31</reference>.
entries.186115fa7800b07c72c35d436439d7c007c5f38b: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen41841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41842" type="x-p"/> And the passover - was nigh - This happened about ten or twelve days before the third passover which Christ celebrated after his baptism. Calmet. For a particular account of our Lord's four passovers see the note on <reference osisRef="Joh.2.13">Joh 2:13</reference>. <div eID="gen41842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41843" type="x-p"/> For thirty days before the Passover there were great preparations made by the Jews, but especially in the last nineteen days, in order to celebrate the feast with due solemnity. Lightfoot supposes that what is here related happened within the last fifteen days. See Calmet's opinion above.
entries.b3df851cfca47505f0e16fc12a2f6caaa17d6d9d: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen41843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41844" type="x-p"/> Saw a great company - See this miracle explained at large on <reference osisRef="Mat.14.13">Mat 14:13</reference> (note), etc.; <reference osisRef="Mar.6.31">Mar 6:31</reference> (note), etc.; <reference osisRef="Luk.9.10">Luk 9:10</reference> (note), etc. In speaking of the passovers, and various other matters, it does not appear that John follows any strict chronological order. From <reference osisRef="Joh.6.15">Joh 6:15</reference>, it appears that our Lord had come down from the mountain, and fed the multitudes in a plain at the foot of it. <div eID="gen41844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41845" type="x-p"/> Saith unto Philip - This, with what follows, to the end of the seventh verse, is not mentioned by any of the other evangelists. <div eID="gen41845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41846" type="x-p"/> Philip was probably the provider for the disciples, as Judas was the treasurer. <div eID="gen41846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41847" type="x-p"/> Whence shall we buy bread - Instead of αγορασομεν, shall we buy, I should read αγορασωμεν, may we buy, which is the reading of ABDEHLS, Mt. VB, and many others. As Philip was of Bethsaida, <reference osisRef="Joh.1.44">Joh 1:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joh.12.21">Joh 12:21</reference>, he must have been much better acquainted with the country in which they then were than any other of the disciples.
entries.48b2dd6d4e7cf131a64d4cecbe870e6f2cdc0fa1: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen41847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41848" type="x-p"/> This he said to prove him - To try his faith, and to see whether he and the other apostles had paid proper attention to the miracles which they had already seen him work; and to draw their attention more particularly to that which he was now about to perform. This is an observation of the evangelist himself, who often interweaves his own judgment with the facts he relates, which St. Matthew rarely ever does. The other evangelists say that, previously to this miracle, he continued to instruct and heal the multitudes till it was near the close of the day. <reference osisRef="Mat.14.14">Mat 14:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.14.15">Mat 14:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mar.6.34">Mar 6:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.6.35">Mar 6:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luk.9.11">Luk 9:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.9.12">Luk 9:12</reference>.
entries.246b8c263d6513ae31ec3f906e016a94623606b1: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen41848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41849" type="x-p"/> Two hundred pennyworth - This sum, rating the denarius at 7 3/4d., would amount to 6. 9s. 2d. of our money, and appears to have been more than our Lord and all his disciples were worth of this world's goods. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Mat.18.28">Mat 18:28</reference>.
entries.7c80b683c295592cdd59c90c748fdeeffdddb619: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen41849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41850" type="x-p"/> Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, saith - The other evangelists attribute this answer to the apostles in general. See the passages referred to above.
entries.62f8f0f6b3930f95a7429423a5a9ce0683c4857f: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen41850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41851" type="x-p"/> There is a lad here - Παιδαριον, a little boy, or servant, probably one who carried the apostles' provisions, or who came on purpose to sell his bread and fish. <div eID="gen41851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41852" type="x-p"/> Five barley loaves - Barley scarcely bore one-third of the value of wheat in the east: see <reference osisRef="Rev.6.6">Rev 6:6</reference>. That it was a very mean fare appears from <reference osisRef="Eze.13.19">Eze 13:19</reference>, where the false prophetesses are said to pollute the name of God for handfuls of barley, i.e. for the meanest reward. And Plutarch, in Apoph. p. 174, speaking concerning the flight of Artaxerxes Mnemon, says he was reduced to such distress as to be obliged to eat barley bread. See Kypke. From this and other circumstances we may plainly perceive that the self-denying doctrine preached by Christ and his apostles was fully exemplified in their own manner of living. <div eID="gen41852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41853" type="x-p"/> Two small fishes - Δυο οψαρια. The word of οψαριον signifies whatever is eaten with bread, to perfect the meal, or to make it easy of deglutition, or to help the digestion. There is no word in the English language for it, which is a great defect. The inhabitants of Scotland, and of the north and north-west of Ireland, use the word kytshen, by which they express what ever is eaten with bread or potatoes, as flesh, fish, butter, milk, eggs, etc., no satisfactory etymology of which word I am able to offer. In the parallel places in the other three evangelists, instead of οψαρια, ιχθυας is used; so that the word evidently means fish in the text of St. John: see on <reference osisRef="Joh.21.5">Joh 21:5</reference> (note).
entries.96237ae41cb16c3349c0970c6f5e95aefb30a51a: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen41853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41854" type="x-p"/> There was much grass in the place - Perhaps newly mown grass, or hay, is meant, (so the Vulgate faenum), and this circumstance marks out more particularly that the passover was at hand. In Palestine the grass is ready for mowing in March; and this miracle seems to have been wrought only a few days before the commencement of that festival: see <reference osisRef="Joh.6.4">Joh 6:4</reference>.
entries.ff00a264419ee76890a3583d3173f87c39470e83: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen41854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41855" type="x-p"/> Jesus took the loaves - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Mat.14.19-Mat.14.21">Mat 14:19-21</reference> (note). As there were five loaves and five thousand people, so there was one loaf to every thousand men, independently of the women and children.
entries.7ae6535d43ad323d9422acec4695d73baaf3a813: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen41855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41856" type="x-p"/> Gather up the fragments - "Great will be the punishment of those who waste the crumbs of food, scatter seed, and neglect the law." Synops Sohar. Among the Jews the פאה peah, or residue after a meal, was the property of the servitors.
entries.25811dbd7f73830f6da483f712c95d990fcf01c9: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen41856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41857" type="x-p"/> This is of a truth that prophet - Spoken of, <reference osisRef="Deu.18.15">Deu 18:15</reference>, viz. the Messiah. How near were these people at this time to the kingdom of heaven!
entries.def9f355c1f6e43ae0ec565f1853d8019e4d2851: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen41857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41858" type="x-p"/> Take him by force, to make him a king - The Jews had often suffered by famine in those times in which their enemies were permitted to prevail over them; but, finding that Jesus had such power as to multiply a few loaves to feed thousands, they took it for granted that while he was at their head no evil could possibly happen to them, and therefore were determined immediately to proclaim him king, and rid themselves at once of Herod and the Romans. Our Lord perceiving this, either by some words which they had dropped, or by his penetration of their hearts, retired before the project had been fully formed, or could be put into execution. It was not till a considerable time afterwards that even the disciples fully understood that his kingdom was not of this world. <div eID="gen41858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41859" type="x-p"/> Into a mountain - That on which he was with his disciples previously to his working this miracle: see <reference osisRef="Joh.6.3">Joh 6:3</reference>. <div eID="gen41859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41860" type="x-p"/> St. Matthew, <reference osisRef="Mat.14.22">Mat 14:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.14.23">Mat 14:23</reference>, and Mark, <reference osisRef="Mar.6.45">Mar 6:45</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.6.46">Mar 6:46</reference>, say that, before this, Jesus constrained his disciples to embark in the vessel, and go along the sea coast towards Capernaum, or Bethsaida - see here <reference osisRef="Joh.6.17">Joh 6:17</reference>, and the note on <reference osisRef="Mar.6.45">Mar 6:45</reference> (note); and that, after they were gone, he dismissed the multitudes, having, no doubt, given them such advices as the nature of the case required; after which he went into the mountain to pray. <div eID="gen41860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41861" type="x-p"/> Worldly wisdom would have said, "Declare thyself king: yield to the desires of the people: this will be the readiest way of converting the Jews." No. Jesus must die for the sin of the world. - No man's heart can be turned to God by outward pomp or splendor - no saving change can be brought about by any might or any power, but by the Spirit of the Lord of hosts. <reference osisRef="Zac.4.6">Zac 4:6</reference>.
entries.c9ee2449b4f912d70bfe4f0e824fdc969963c071: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen41861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41862" type="x-p"/> Toward Capernaum - St. Mark says, <reference osisRef="Mar.6.45">Mar 6:45</reference>, that our Lord commanded them to go along to Bethsaida; and in the course of the history we find they got neither to Bethsaida nor Capernaum, but landed in the country of Genesaret: <reference osisRef="Mat.14.34">Mat 14:34</reference>. Our Lord seems to have desired them to go either to Bethsaida or Capernaum, which were only a very few miles distant, and on the same side of the sea. The reason why they could reach neither was the storm which the evangelists say rose at the time, and the wind being contrary: the storm being probably excited by the prince of the power of the air. Capernaum lay at the northern part of this sea, and they went along the Galilean or western coast, probably expecting Christ to come to them, on which account they might keep in close by the land. But there are great difficulties in fixing the places mentioned by the evangelists. By some writers Bethsaida and Capernaum are placed on opposite sides of this lake: by others on the same side. Sometimes when our translation speaks of passing over the sea, etc., a coasting voyage only is meant, as we find the disciples landing on the same side from which they had departed: see the note on <reference osisRef="Joh.6.22">Joh 6:22</reference>.
entries.1e9f0522d437e172efb2ee87da55a80a9dd9dc3d: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen41862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41863" type="x-p"/> Had rowed - Their vessel was a small one only, something of the boat kind: as to sails, if they had any, they could not now venture to carry them, because of the storm. <div eID="gen41863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41864" type="x-p"/> Five and twenty or thirty furlongs - Between three and four miles. The sea of Tiberias, on which they now were, was, according to Josephus, War, book iii. chap. 25, forty furlongs, or five miles in breadth; and one hundred and forty furlongs, or eighteen miles, in length. Pliny, lib. v. chap. 15, makes it about six miles broad, and sixteen long. <div eID="gen41864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41865" type="x-p"/> They see Jesus - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Mat.14.25">Mat 14:25</reference>, etc.
entries.0aa3386f5d683afa8456872748ef8f3c1aa8a668: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen41865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41866" type="x-p"/> Immediately the ship was at the land - How far they were from the place at which they landed, when our Lord came to them, we know not. But the evangelist seems to speak of their sudden arrival there as extraordinary and miraculous.
entries.d6f7ec556bfc8fea3eea973801c0f30eeed8f8d8: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen41866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41867" type="x-p"/> The people which stood on the other side - ἙϚηκως περαν της θαλασσης, Standing by the sea side. The people were not on the other side, i.e. in Perea, as our version states, but on that side where Bethsaida lay: see the notes on <reference osisRef="Mat.14.25">Mat 14:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.14.34">Mat 14:34</reference>, and on <reference osisRef="Mar.6.45">Mar 6:45</reference>. The Greek word, περαν, says Bishop Pearce, seems to signify in Scripture sometimes on the side of, and sometimes on this side of: see <reference osisRef="Jos.5.1">Jos 5:1</reference> and 1 Maccabees 9:34. The Hebrew word אבר abar, signifies by the side: <reference osisRef="Exo.28.26">Exo 28:26</reference>, and is translated on this side in <reference osisRef="Deu.4.29">Deu 4:29</reference>. It has the same meaning in the Septuagint, <reference osisRef="Deu.1.5">Deu 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.3.8">Deu 3:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.4.46">Deu 4:46</reference>. περαν, says Vorstius, is the same with παρα, near to. This is evidently the meaning of the word in <reference osisRef="Mat.4.15">Mat 4:15</reference>; as it appears, from what is said of the land of Zabulon and Nepthali, that by περαν is not meant beyond, but by the side of; because those two tribes inhabited the western side of Jordan, which was the side lying nearest to Judea and Galilee: see on <reference osisRef="Mat.19.1">Mat 19:1</reference> (note).
entries.f165249a3e48c9310a2377b944c8c479cb9a85a4: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen41867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41868" type="x-p"/> There came other boats - After Jesus and his disciples had departed. <div eID="gen41868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41869" type="x-p"/> From Tiberias - Herod Antipas built this city near the lake of Genesaret, in the best parts of Galilee, and called it Tiberias, in honor of Tiberius, the Roman emperor: see Jos. Ant. book xviii. chap. 2. sect. 3.
entries.6510c9103569c99dc6b0144ccc658c85a1a5f4e3: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen41869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41870" type="x-p"/> They also took shipping - That is, as many of them as could get accommodated with boats took them and thus got to Capernaum; but many others doubtless went thither on foot, as it is not at all likely that five or six thousand persons could get boats enow to carry them.
entries.479bab6fa4af47079e853d748394f6b9a3ba4211: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen41870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41871" type="x-p"/> On the other side of the sea - That is, on the sea coast, to the northward of it, where Capernaum lies in the land of Genesaret: but see the note, on <reference osisRef="Joh.6.17">Joh 6:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.22">Joh 6:22</reference>. It was in one of the synagogues of Capernaum that he delivered the following discourse: see <reference osisRef="Joh.6.59">Joh 6:59</reference>.
entries.75600c49e82fd5e393e4aefa301462a87aeb7569: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen41871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41872" type="x-p"/> Ye seek me, not because ye saw, etc. - Though the miracle of the loaves was one of the most astonishing that ever was wrought upon earth; and though this people had, by the testimony of all their senses, the most convincing proof of its reality; yet we find many of them paid little attention to it, and regarded the omnipotent hand of God in it no farther than it went to satisfy the demands of their appetite! Most men are willing to receive temporal good from the hands of God; but there are few, very few, who are willing to receive spiritual blessings.
entries.dd6058c7ee61a93963fd5049a075b4972833ba6c: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen41872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41873" type="x-p"/> Labor not for the meat - That is, for that only, but also for the bread, etc. Our Lord wills every man to be active and diligent in that employment in which providence has placed him; but it is his will also that that employment, and all the concerns of life, should be subservient to the interest of his soul. <div eID="gen41873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41874" type="x-p"/> But for that meat, etc. - He who labors not, in the work of his salvation, is never likely to enter into the kingdom of God. Though our labor cannot purchase it, either in whole or in part, yet it is the way in which God chooses to give salvation; and he that will have heaven must strive for it. Every thing that can be possessed, except the salvation of God, is a perishing thing: this is its essential character: it can last to us no longer than the body lasts. But, when the earth and its produce are burnt up, this bread of Christ, his grace and salvation, will be found remaining unto eternal life. This is the portion after which an immortal spirit should seek. <div eID="gen41874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41875" type="x-p"/> Him hath God the Father sealed - By this expression, our Lord points out the commission which, as the Messiah, he received from the Father, to be prophet and priest to an ignorant, sinful world. As a person who wishes to communicate his mind to another who is at a distance writes a letter, seals it with his own seal, and sends it directed to the person for whom it was written, so Christ, who lay in the bosom of the Father, came to interpret the Divine will to man, bearing the image, superscription, and seal of God, in the immaculate holiness of his nature, unsullied truth of his doctrine, and in the astonishing evidence of his miracles. But he came also as a priest, to make an atonement for sin; and the bread which nourishes unto eternal life, he tells us, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.51">Joh 6:51</reference>, is his body, which he gives for the life of the world; and to this sacrifice of himself, the words, him hath God the Father sealed, seem especially to relate. It certainly was a custom, among nations contiguous to Judea, to set a seal upon the victim which was deemed proper for sacrifice. The following account of the method of providing white bulls among the Egyptians, for sacrifices to their god Apis, taken from Herodotus, Euterpe, b. ii. p. 117, casts much light upon this place. "They sacrifice white bulls to Apis; and for that reason make the following trial. If they find one black hair upon him, they consider him as unclean: that they may know this with certainty, the priest appointed for this purpose views every part of the animal, both standing and lying on the ground. After this, he draws out his tongue, to see if he be clean by certain signs: in the last place, he looks upon the hairs of his tail, that he may be sure they are as by nature they should be. If, after this search, the bull is found unblemished, he signifies it by tying a label to his horns; then, having applied wax, he seals it with his ring, and they lead him away: for it is death to sacrifice one of these animals, unless he have been marked with such a seal. <div eID="gen41875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41876" type="x-p"/> The Jews could not be unacquainted with the rites and ceremonies of the Egyptian worship; and it is possible that such precautions as these were in use among themselves, especially as they were so strictly enjoined to have their sacrifices without Spot, and without blemish. Infinite justice found Jesus Christ to be without spot or blemish, and therefore sealed, pointed out and accepted him, as a proper sacrifice and atonement for the sin of the whole world. Collate with this passage, <reference osisRef="Heb.7.26-Heb.7.28">Heb 7:26-28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.27">Eph 5:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.14">2Pet 3:14</reference>; and especially <reference osisRef="Heb.9.13">Heb 9:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.14">Heb 9:14</reference> : For if the blood of Bulls and of goats, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkling the unclean, sanctifieth - how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself Without Spot to God, purge your consciences from dead works! The rabbins talk much of the seal of God, which they suppose to be אמת emeth, or truth; and that this is a representation of the unoriginated and endless perfections of God. This doctrine is just; but their method of proving it is not so satisfactory. Aleph א, say they, is the first letter of the alphabet; mem מ the middle; and tau ת the last: these three letters make אמת emeth, Truth, because God is the first - there was none before him; he is the middle - none mingles with him; and he is the last - there can be none after him. Hieros. Sanhed. fol. 18. See also <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.18">1Pet 1:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.19">1Pet 1:19</reference>.
entries.0e898128d6ace7eb86bd5502bd0eeb3884c04633: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen41876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41877" type="x-p"/> That we might work the works of God? - That is, Divine works, or such as God can approve.
entries.943d6c1a5725ae9939fd03cbf5cd8a7d6a324d4d: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen41877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41878" type="x-p"/> This is the work of God, that ye believe - There is nothing you can be employed in more acceptable to God than in yielding to the evidence set before you, and acknowledging me as your Messiah and the Savior of a lost world.
entries.b65a8077d3211f2a2d5d37b14087f488e52a30ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen41878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41879" type="x-p"/> What sign - Τι σημειον, What miracle; so the word is evidently used, <reference osisRef="Joh.2.11">Joh 2:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.2.23">Joh 2:23</reference>, and in many other places. <div eID="gen41879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41880" type="x-p"/> That we may see, and believe thee - That, having seen the miracle, we may believe thee to be the promised Messiah. They had already seen the miracle of the five loaves, and did not believe; and it was impossible for them to see any thing more descriptive of unlimited power and goodness. Even miracles themselves are lost on persons whose hearts are fixed on the perishing things of the world, and whose minds are filled with prejudice against the truth.
entries.7326ba06bed1ecde6a790947acada773073b3524: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen41880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41881" type="x-p"/> Our fathers did eat manna in the desert - Their argument seems to run thus: Thou hast, we grant, fed five thousand men with five loaves and two small fishes; but what is this in comparison of what Moses did in the desert, who for forty years fed more than a million of persons with bread from heaven: do something like this, and then we will believe in thee, as we have believed in Moses.
entries.17b63678e66391dbc95ef051776ec56ddc7e21c4: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen41881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41882" type="x-p"/> Moses gave you not that bread from heaven - Our Lord refutes the argument of the Jews, by proving: <div eID="gen41882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41883" type="x-p"/> 1. That it was not Moses, but God, who gave the manna. <div eID="gen41883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41884" type="x-p"/> 2. That this bread was not the true bread, but was merely a type of it. <div eID="gen41884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41885" type="x-p"/> 3. That God had given them now a bread infinitely more excellent. <div eID="gen41885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41886" type="x-p"/> 4. That himself is that heavenly nourishment of which he spake, and who was typified by the manna in the desert. <div eID="gen41886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41887" type="x-p"/> To show that himself was the true bread from heaven, he proves two things: <div eID="gen41887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41888" type="x-p"/> 1. That his doctrine was the true nourishment of the soul, and that those who were to be put in possession of the blessings promised in it must come to God by faith. <div eID="gen41888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41889" type="x-p"/> 2. That he would give his body for the life of the world: that as bread is the staff that supports the natural life of man, so the salvation procured by his death should be that by which the bodies and souls of believers should be preserved unto life eternal.
entries.e23cb27148b5683e07b012b000bcfa53c6e15e73: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen41889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41890" type="x-p"/> Lord, evermore give us this bread - Either meaning, "Let the miracle of the manna be renewed, and continue among us for ever:" or, "Let that bread of which thou hast spoken, become our constant nourishment." The Jews expected that, when the Messiah should come, he would give them all manner of delicacies, and, among the rest, manna, wine, and spicy oil. From the following extract, we may see where Mohammed got his Paradise. "Many affirm, says Rab. Mayemon, that the hope of Israel is this: That the Messiah shall come and raise the dead; and they shall be gathered together in the garden of Eden, and shall eat and drink and satiate themselves all the days of the world. There the houses shall be all builded with precious stones; the beds shall be made of silk; and the rivers shall flow with wine and spicy oil. He made manna to descend for them, in which was all manner of tastes; and every Israelite found in it what his palate was chiefly pleased with. If he desired fat in it, he had it. In it, the young man tasted bread, the old man honey, and the children oil. So shall it be in the world to come, (i.e. the days of the Messiah.) He shall give Israel peace, and they shall sit down in the garden of Eden, and all nations shall behold their condition; as it is said, My servants shall eat, but ye shall be hungry, etc., <reference osisRef="Isa.65.13">Isa 65:13</reference>." See Lightfoot.
entries.cf3be3023d401de6b4ca6d111ddd02bd0ab691e3: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen41890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41891" type="x-p"/> I am the bread of life - That is, the bread which gives life, and preserves from death. <div eID="gen41891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41892" type="x-p"/> He that cometh to me - The person who receives my doctrine, and believes in me as the great atoning sacrifice, shall be perfectly satisfied, and never more feel misery of mind. All the guilt of his sins shall be blotted out, and his soul shall be purified unto God; and, being enabled to love him with all his heart, he shall rest, fully, supremely, and finally happy, in his God.
entries.1c43011664a6507cdba20b159845e62012926b40: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen41892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41893" type="x-p"/> All that the Father giveth me - The neuter gender, παν, is probably used here for the masculine, πας. <div eID="gen41893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41894" type="x-p"/> Shall come to me - All that are drawn by the Father, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.44">Joh 6:44</reference>, i.e. all those who are influenced by his Spirit, and yield to those influences: for as many as are Led (not driven or dragged) by the Spirit of God, they are the children of God, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.14">Rom 8:14</reference>. God sent his prophets to proclaim his salvation to this people; and he accompanied their preaching with the influence of his Spirit. Those who yielded were saved: those who did not yield to these drawings were lost. This Spirit still continued to work and to allure; but the people being uncircumcised both in heart and ears, they always resisted the Holy Ghost; as their fathers did, so did they; <reference osisRef="Act.7.51">Act 7:51</reference>. And though Christ would have gathered them together, as a hen would her chickens under her wings, yet they would not. See the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.23.37">Mat 23:37</reference>. Those who come at the call of God, he is represented here as giving to Christ, because it is through his blood alone that they can be saved. God, by his Spirit, convinces of sin, righteousness, and judgment; those who acknowledge their iniquity, and their need of salvation, he gives to Christ, i.e. points out unto them the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. Our Lord may here also refer to the calling of the Gentiles; for these, according to the ancient promise, <reference osisRef="Psa.2.8">Psa 2:8</reference>, were given to Christ: and they, on the preaching of the Gospel, gladly came unto him. See ample proofs of this in the Acts of the Apostles. <div eID="gen41894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41895" type="x-p"/> I will in no wise cast out - The words are exceedingly emphatical - ου μη εκβαλω εξω, I will by no means thrust out of doors; excellently rendered by Matthew of Erberg in his Italian Bible - Io non cacciaro fuori, I will not chase him out of the house. Our blessed Lord alludes to the case of a person in deep distress and poverty, who comes to a nobleman's house, in order to get relief: the person appears; and the owner, far from treating the poor man with asperity, welcomes, receives him kindly, and supplies his wants. So does Jesus. Newer did he reject the suit of a penitent, however grievous his crimes might have been. He is come to the house of mercy; he is lying at the threshold: the servants bid him come in - he obeys, and stands trembling, waiting for the appearing of the Master, doubtful whether he is to be received or rejected: the Master appears, and not only grants his suit, but receives him into the number of his family: he alleges his unfitness, his unworthiness, his guilt, his crimes, his ingratitude: no matter, all shall be blotted out through the blood of the Lamb, and he be put among the children, and on none of these accounts shall he be put out of the house. The Gentiles shall be as welcome as the Jews; and the invitation to them be as free, as full, and as hearty: they shall become his adopted children, and never be cast out, as the Jews have been. O thou God of love! how able and Willing art thou to save the vilest of the vile, who come unto thee! Thou art not the God of the Jews only, thou art also the God of the Gentiles. Rejoice, therefore, ye Gentiles, with his people.
entries.7b0bbd6c869ee42ef2838add58a186736b0325c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen41895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41896" type="x-p"/> Not to do mine own will - I am come, not to act according to human motives, passions, or prejudices; but according to infinite wisdom, goodness, and mercy. Jewish passions and prejudices would reject publicans and sinners as those alluded to, and shut the gate of heaven against the Gentiles; but God's mercy receives them, and I am come to manifest that mercy to men.
entries.b6f20bc315c0d8e2247bbe6e925156a433ed87b9: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen41896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41897" type="x-p"/> I should lose nothing - It is the will of God that every soul who believes should continue in the faith, and have a resurrection unto life eternal. But he wills this continuance in salvation, without purposing to force the persons so to continue. God may will a thing to be, without willing that it shall be. Judas was given to Christ by the Father, <reference osisRef="Joh.17.12">Joh 17:12</reference>. The Father willed that this Judas should continue in the faith, and have a resurrection unto life eternal: but Judas sinned and perished. Now it is evident that God willed that Judas might be saved, without willing that he must be saved infallibly and unconditionally. When a man is a worker together with the grace of God, he is saved; when he receives that grace of God in vain, he is lost - not through a lack of will or mercy in God, but through lack of his co-operation with Divine grace. God saves no man as a stock or a stone, but as a reasonable being and free agent. "That which thou hast heard, thou mayest hold fast, and persevere in, if thou wilt," Says St. Augustin. In eo quod audieras, et tenueras, perseverares, si velles. De Correct. &Grat. c. 7. See Calmet. <div eID="gen41897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41898" type="x-p"/> Raise it up again at the last day - The Jews believed that the wicked should have no resurrection; and that the principle that led to the resurrection of the body, in the righteous, was the indwelling Spirit of God. This is positively asserted in the Shir Hashirim Rabba. See Schoettgen.
entries.7eb5c63f53012c779b436f9ab1c0a974f5952bb2: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen41898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41899" type="x-p"/> This is the will of him that sent me - Lest they should take a wrong meaning out of his words, as many have done since, he tells them that, far from any person being excluded from his mercy, it was the will of God that every one who saw him might believe and be saved. The power, without which they could not believe, he freely gave them; but the use of that power was their own. God gives the grace of repentance and faith to every man; but he neither repents nor believes for any man. Each must repent for his own sins, and believe in the Lord Jesus, through the grace given, or perish.
entries.25f18837d05615a65173a9ec8110fd1b3284d274: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen41899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41900" type="x-p"/> The Jews then murmured - Because the whole of his discourse event to prove that he was infinitely greater than Moses; and that he alone could give present peace and eternal glory to men.
entries.3631a9fc8893702cfbbf57ac63933b02c9f98e6a: <hi type="bold">Verse 44</hi> <div eID="gen41900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41901" type="x-p"/> Except the Father - draw him - But how is a man drawn? St. Augustin answers from the poet, Trahit sua quemque voluptas; a man is attracted by that which he delights in. Show green herbage to a sheep, he is drawn by it: show nuts to a child, and he is drawn by them. They run wherever the person runs who shows these things: they run after him, but they are not forced to follow; they run, through the desire they feel to get the things they delight in. So God draws man: he shows him his wants - he shows the Savior whom he has provided for him: the man feels himself a lost sinner; and, through the desire which he finds to escape hell, and get to heaven, he comes unto Christ, that he may be justified by his blood. Unless God thus draw, no man will ever come to Christ; because none could, without this drawing, ever feel the need of a Savior. See August. Tract. 26, in Joan. and Calmet. <div eID="gen41901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41902" type="x-p"/> Drawing, or alluring, not dragging is here to be understood.
